title: Milestones
objective: Students will read the Black Barbie Timeline, from Francie (1967) to today, and put its stops in order. They will learn that the first Black Barbie, introduced by Mattel in 1980, was designed by Kitty Black Perkins, a Black fashion designer at Mattel, and say what made it new. They will tell the poster’s words from a museum note, and explain how one doll built on the dolls before it.

objectives.heading: By the end of this lesson you will be able to:
objectives.why: A timeline shows how things change, and who changed them. This one shows toys changing to reflect more of the children who play with them, and a Black designer at the center of that change.

materials: Page 3 of this plan; its eight stop cards, cut apart
questions: Which stop do you think was the biggest change? Why?
The poster calls Francie and Christie *problematic*. What do you think it means?
Why do you think the first Black Barbie mattered to the children who played with it?
If you could add a stop for next year, what doll would you want to see?
questionsLabel: Questions to ask in front of the timeline
connection: **Online,** the Black Barbie Timeline asks students to guess the year at each stop and ends with a final challenge: from clues in the poster and the museum's notes, did each doll come before or after the first Black Barbie? **In the exhibition,** the display case holds the Nigerian and Ghanaian boxed editions and the three Inspiring Women dolls.

steps.title: A road through time
script: Show the Black Barbie Timeline and say nothing yet. Ask: *“What do you notice? What do you think a timeline shows?”* Draw out that a timeline puts events in order by when they happened.

screen.alt: The Black Barbie Timeline room: 1967 and Francie in a ringed circle on the lime ground, a right guess, and the years still to find along a road below
screen.caption: *The Black Barbie Timeline*

steps.purpose: Look first: what is a timeline for, and what might this one show?
students: What do you think a timeline shows?

steps.title: Guess the year
script: Then play the timeline’s own game: *“Mattel made the first Black Barbie. When was it? 1971, 1976, 1980 or 1989?”* Students vote with fingers, one to four, and give a reason. Leave the answer for a moment.

screen.question: Mattel made the first Black Barbie. When was it?

steps.purpose: Guess before being told, as the timeline itself asks.

steps.title: Eight stops
script: Reveal the answer: **1980**, *“a significant milestone in toy manufacturing and cultural representation,”* as poster 2 says. Read the eight stops from the chart on page 3. Two Black dolls came first: Francie in 1967 and Christie in 1968. Read: *“Christie was presented as part of Barbie’s friend group, while Francie was essentially a white doll design with darker skin.”* The poster calls these earlier efforts *problematic*: ask students why.

screen.caption: The Black Barbie Timeline: eight stops

cells: One of Mattel’s two earlier Black dolls: “essentially a white doll design with darker skin”
The other earlier Black doll: “presented as part of Barbie’s friend group”
Designed by Kitty Black Perkins: Afrocentric facial features, natural hairstyles, a glamorous design
A Nigerian Barbie (about 1990) and a Ghanaian Barbie (1996); boxed editions of both are in the display case
Designed by Kitty Black Perkins: Mattel’s first line of Black fashion dolls launched separately from the Barbie line
AKA Centennial Barbie and “So In Style”
Authentic Black features and realistic hair textures
Dolls honoring Ida B. Wells, Madam C. J. Walker and Bessie Coleman; all three are in the display case
“A cherished collector’s item and a symbol of the ongoing journey toward equality and representation”

steps.purpose: Read the timeline from start to end, and find 1980 on it.

steps.title: Kitty Black Perkins
script: Read: *“The first Black Barbie, however, was a groundbreaking creation designed by Kitty Black Perkins, a trailblazing Black fashion designer at Mattel. This doll broke away from past missteps, featuring Afrocentric facial features, natural hairstyles, and a glamorous design that celebrated Black beauty.”* *Afrocentric* means centered on Africa and people of African descent. Ask: *“Why might it matter that a Black designer made this doll?”*

screen.text: The first Black Barbie, however, was a groundbreaking creation designed by Kitty Black Perkins, a trailblazing Black fashion designer at Mattel.

steps.purpose: Meet the designer, and hear what made her doll new.
students: Who designed the first Black Barbie?
What three things were new about it?

steps.title: Poster or museum note?
script: Most stops quote poster 2. Three do not: Dolls of the World, Shani and Inspiring Women. On the timeline they are marked *“A museum note, not the poster’s words”*, and each names its source in the timeline’s Sources list. Ask: *“The poster’s words, or a museum note: why does a museum say where a fact comes from?”* A source lets anyone check a fact.

screen.question: The poster’s words, or a museum note: why does a museum say where a fact comes from?

steps.purpose: Tell the poster’s words from the museum’s added notes, and see why sources matter.
students: Which three stops are museum notes?

steps.title: Choose a handout
script: Students choose a handout. All three levels put the stops in order and find what made the first Black Barbie new.

levels.name: Green Level
levels.summary: Read a printed timeline to answer questions, match four dolls to what was new about each, circle what made the first Black Barbie new, and draw a doll for a stop still to come.

levels.name: Yellow Level
levels.summary: Number eight shuffled stop cards in order, finish a timeline table from a fact file, sort the stops into the poster’s words and museum notes, and explain why the designer mattered.

levels.name: Red Level
levels.summary: Order the stops and work out the years between them, explain what the poster finds problematic about Francie, show how one doll built on another, and plan research on an Inspiring Women doll.

steps.purpose: Read the timeline independently, at the right level of challenge.
students: Choose Green, Yellow or Red. All three put the stops in order and find what made the first Black Barbie new.

steps.section: A human timeline and look back
steps.title: A human timeline
script: Give eight students the stop cards from page 3, each folded so only the name shows. The class puts them in order, earliest first; then the eight unfold their cards and check by the years.

screen.question: Eight stops, eight people: can the class put them in order?

steps.purpose: Put the stops in order from memory, then check by the years.
students: Hold your card with the year hidden.
Earliest at one end, today at the other.

steps.section: A human timeline and look back
steps.title: Look back
script: Ask the objectives back, from the screen or page 1: *“Can you now…?”* Students show a thumb up, sideways or down. Exit question: *“Name one milestone and say what changed.”*

screen.hint: Show me: thumb up, sideways or down.
